project_brief: Build a command-line application to run a small snacks and lemonade stand business. You'll create a modular Python program that tracks inventory, processes customer orders with validation, generates receipts, and ranks your best customers—all while saving data to JSON files so nothing gets lost between sessions.

milestones.description: Create your project folder with two empty Python files: 'main.py' and 'store_manager.py'. Think of this like setting up two workstations—one for the cashier (main.py handles talking to customers) and one for the back office (store_manager.py handles all the behind-the-scenes inventory math). You'll also create a blank 'inventory.json' file to understand where your data will live.

tasks.instruction_theory: Every coding project needs a home—a folder where all your files live together. Think of it like creating a drawer for your lemonade stand paperwork. This folder will hold your Python code files and your data files. Having everything in one place keeps you organized and makes sure Python can find all the pieces it needs when running your program.
coding_requirements: Create a new folder named 'lemonade_stand' on your computer
This folder will be your project root directory where all files will be stored
hints: You can create folders using your computer's file explorer, or right-click and select 'New Folder'
Pick a location you'll remember, like your Desktop or Documents folder
Avoid spaces in folder names—use underscores instead (lemonade_stand, not lemonade stand)

milestones.description: In 'store_manager.py', create your InventoryManager class with an __init__ method that sets up an empty list to hold inventory items. This is like building an empty filing cabinet before you fill it with folders. You'll learn how a class acts as a blueprint that remembers things (your inventory) and can do tasks (load, save, update).

Creating a separate file called 'store_manager.py' keeps your code organized—like having a drawer just for inventory stuff, separate from the drawer where you'll handle customer interactions later. This separation makes your code easier to read and fix when something goes wrong.

tasks.instruction_theory: A class in Python is like a blueprint or a cookie cutter. Imagine you want to make lots of identical cookies—you don't reshape each one by hand, you use a cookie cutter! A class defines what something IS and what it CAN DO. Your InventoryManager class will be the blueprint for an object that knows how to handle all your inventory tasks. The 'class' keyword tells Python: 'Hey, I'm defining a new type of thing here!'

Use the 'class' keyword followed by the class name and a colon

tasks.instruction_theory: The __init__ method is like the 'setup instructions' that run automatically when you create a new object from your class. Think of it like this: when you buy a new phone, it goes through a setup process the first time you turn it on. The __init__ method is that setup process for your class. The 'self' parameter is how the object refers to itself—like saying 'my own inventory list' instead of 'someone else's inventory list'. Every method inside a class needs 'self' as its first parameter.
coding_requirements: Replace 'pass' with a method named '__init__'
The __init__ method must take 'self' as its first (and only) parameter

hints: The method name has two underscores before AND after 'init': __init__
Don't forget 'self' in the parentheses—it's required!

When you write 'self.inventory = []', you're saying 'this specific InventoryManager object has its own inventory list.' The empty list [] is like an empty filing cabinet—ready to hold inventory items later. This is different from a regular variable because it 'belongs' to the object and sticks around as long as the object exists.

When you write 'manager = InventoryManager()', Python calls your __init__ method automatically and creates a brand new InventoryManager object. This object now has its own inventory list and knows which file to use. You can create multiple managers if you wanted (like having separate filing cabinets for different stores), and each would have its own independent inventory. milestones.subheading_title: Load Inventory from JSON with Fallback Defaults
milestones.description: Add a 'load_inventory' method to your class that reads from 'inventory.json'. Here's the clever part: if the file doesn't exist yet, your code creates it with starter items (Lemonade at $2.50, Cookies at $1.00, Chips at $1.50). This prevents crashes and means your stand is never empty on day one. You'll use try/except to handle the 'file not found' situation gracefully.

tasks.instruction_theory: Before we can load anything, we need to know what our 'starter kit' looks like. Think of this like having a backup box of supplies in your garage—if your main inventory is missing, you grab the backup. In Python, we store this as a list of dictionaries. Each dictionary represents one product with its name, price, and how many you have in stock.
coding_requirements: Inside your InventoryManager class in 'store_manager.py', create a class attribute called 'DEFAULT_INVENTORY'
Set it equal to a list containing three dictionaries
First dict: {'name': 'Lemonade', 'price': 2.50, 'quantity': 10}
Second dict: {'name': 'Cookies', 'price': 1.00, 'quantity': 20}
Third dict: {'name': 'Chips', 'price': 1.50, 'quantity': 15}
hints: Class attributes go right under the 'class InventoryManager:' line, before __init__
Make sure price values are floats (have decimal points like 2.50, not just 2)
You can access this later with self.DEFAULT_INVENTORY or InventoryManager.DEFAULT_INVENTORY

test_specification.expected_state: The InventoryManager class has a DEFAULT_INVENTORY attribute containing exactly 3 items with correct names, prices, and quantities
test_specification.verification_code:
from store_manager import InventoryManager
im = InventoryManager()
assert hasattr(InventoryManager, 'DEFAULT_INVENTORY'), 'Missing DEFAULT_INVENTORY'
defaults = InventoryManager.DEFAULT_INVENTORY
assert len(defaults) == 3, 'Should have 3 default items'
names = [item['name'] for item in defaults]
assert 'Lemonade' in names and 'Cookies' in names and 'Chips' in names, 'Missing required items'
lemonade = next(i for i in defaults if i['name'] == 'Lemonade')
assert lemonade['price'] == 2.50 and lemonade['quantity'] == 10, 'Lemonade has wrong values'

tasks.instruction_theory: Now let's learn how to read JSON files. The 'json' module is like a translator—it converts JSON files (which are just text) into Python lists and dictionaries you can actually work with. The pattern is: open the file, then use json.load() to read and translate it. We'll start by writing the basic file-reading code without error handling first.
coding_requirements: At the top of 'store_manager.py', add 'import json' if not already present
Inside InventoryManager, create a method called 'load_inventory' that takes only 'self' as parameter
Inside the method, use 'open()' with the filename 'inventory.json' and mode 'r' (read)
Use 'json.load()' to read the file contents into a variable
Store the loaded data in 'self.inventory'
hints: The pattern is: with open('filename.json', 'r') as file: data = json.load(file)
Using 'with open()' automatically closes the file when done—it's the safe way
json.load(file) is different from json.loads(string)—load is for files, loads is for strings

test_specification.expected_state: The load_inventory method exists and can read from an existing inventory.json file
test_specification.verification_code:
import json
import os
from store_manager import InventoryManager
test_data = [{'name': 'TestItem', 'price': 5.00, 'quantity': 3}]
with open('inventory.json', 'w') as f:
    json.dump(test_data, f)
im = InventoryManager()
im.load_inventory()
assert hasattr(im, 'inventory'), 'inventory attribute not set'
assert im.inventory[0]['name'] == 'TestItem', 'Did not load correct data'
os.remove('inventory.json')

tasks.instruction_theory: Here's where the magic happens! What if the file doesn't exist? Without protection, Python crashes with a FileNotFoundError. That's like your cash register exploding because someone asked for a receipt before any sales happened—not great! We use try/except to catch this error gracefully. Think of 'try' as saying 'attempt this risky thing' and 'except' as 'if it fails, do this instead'.
coding_requirements: Wrap your existing file-opening code inside a 'try:' block
Add an 'except FileNotFoundError:' block after the try block
In the except block, set 'self.inventory' equal to a copy of 'self.DEFAULT_INVENTORY'
Use 'self.DEFAULT_INVENTORY.copy()' or list slicing '[:]' to make a copy, not a reference
hints: The structure is: try: (risky code) except FileNotFoundError: (backup plan)
Making a copy is important! If you just do self.inventory = self.DEFAULT_INVENTORY, changing one changes both
You can also use 'import copy' and 'copy.deepcopy()' for nested structures, but .copy() works for our list

test_specification.expected_state: When inventory.json doesn't exist, load_inventory uses DEFAULT_INVENTORY instead of crashing
test_specification.verification_code:

from store_manager import InventoryManager
if os.path.exists('inventory.json'):
    os.remove('inventory.json')
im = InventoryManager()
im.load_inventory()
assert hasattr(im, 'inventory'), 'inventory not set'
assert len(im.inventory) == 3, 'Should have 3 default items'
assert im.inventory[0]['name'] == 'Lemonade', 'First item should be Lemonade'

tasks.instruction_theory: When we use the default inventory as a fallback, we should immediately save it to the JSON file. This way, the file gets created for next time, and we have a record of our starting inventory. It's like writing down your backup supplies in your official inventory book so everything stays in sync.
coding_requirements: Inside the 'except FileNotFoundError:' block, after setting self.inventory to defaults
Call 'self.save_inventory()' to write the defaults to 'inventory.json'
This assumes you already have a save_inventory method from Milestone 2
hints: The save happens AFTER you set self.inventory, so save_inventory has data to save
If save_inventory doesn't exist yet, you may need to create it first (check Milestone 2)
This creates the file automatically so next time load_inventory will find it

test_specification.expected_state: When defaults are used, they are automatically saved to inventory.json
test_specification.verification_code:

import json
from store_manager import InventoryManager

    os.remove('inventory.json')
im = InventoryManager()
im.load_inventory()
assert os.path.exists('inventory.json'), 'File should be created'
with open('inventory.json', 'r') as f:
    saved = json.load(f)
assert len(saved) == 3, 'Should save 3 items'
assert saved[0]['name'] == 'Lemonade', 'Should save Lemonade first'
os.remove('inventory.json')

tasks.instruction_theory: Let's also handle the case where the file exists but contains garbage or corrupted data. If someone accidentally messes up the JSON file (maybe they opened it in Notepad and deleted a bracket), we don't want our program to crash. We catch JSONDecodeError to handle this situation and fall back to defaults.
coding_requirements: Add 'json.JSONDecodeError' to your except clause using a tuple: except (FileNotFoundError, json.JSONDecodeError):
This makes the same fallback code run for both missing files AND corrupted files
The rest of the except block stays the same—use defaults and save them
hints: Multiple exceptions in one except use parentheses: except (Error1, Error2):
JSONDecodeError happens when json.load() can't understand the file contents
You could also write two separate except blocks, but combining them is cleaner here

test_specification.expected_state: Corrupted JSON files trigger the fallback to defaults instead of crashing

tasks.instruction_theory: Finally, let's make sure our InventoryManager automatically loads inventory when it's created. By calling load_inventory() inside __init__, we guarantee that any time someone creates an InventoryManager, it's ready to go with data—either from the file or from defaults. It's like a store that automatically checks its shelves when opening for the day.

milestones.description: Create a 'save_inventory' method that writes your current inventory list back to 'inventory.json'. Every time someone buys something, you'll call this method so the stock numbers stay accurate even if you close the program. Think of it like updating your clipboard after each sale so tomorrow's you knows exactly what's left.

tasks.instruction_theory: Before we can save anything, we need to understand how Python writes data to files. Remember how we used 'r' mode to read? Now we'll use 'w' mode (write mode). Here's the cool part: 'w' mode completely replaces whatever was in the file before. It's like erasing your whiteboard and writing fresh info. This is perfect for us because we want to save the CURRENT state of inventory, not add to old data.
coding_requirements: In 'store_manager.py', inside your InventoryManager class, create a new method called 'save_inventory'
The method should take only 'self' as a parameter (no extra inputs needed)
Inside the method, open 'inventory.json' using 'with open()' in write mode ('w')
hints: Write mode looks like: with open('inventory.json', 'w') as file:
Make sure this method is indented inside your class, at the same level as load_inventory
Don't put any code inside the 'with' block yet - we'll do that next

test_specification.expected_state: The InventoryManager class has a save_inventory method that opens inventory.json in write mode
test_specification.verification_code:
import ast
with open('store_manager.py', 'r') as f:
    source = f.read()
    tree = ast.parse(source)
    class_def = [node for node in ast.walk(tree) if isinstance(node, ast.ClassDef) and node.name == 'InventoryManager'][0]
    methods = [node.name for node in class_def.body if isinstance(node, ast.FunctionDef)]
    assert 'save_inventory' in methods, 'save_inventory method not found in InventoryManager'
    assert "'w'" in source or '"w"' in source, 'Write mode not found in code'

tasks.instruction_theory: Now we need to convert our Python list (self.inventory) back into JSON format and write it to the file. The json.dump() function does exactly this - it takes your Python data and writes it directly to a file as JSON. Think of json.load() as 'JSON to Python' and json.dump() as 'Python to JSON'. They're opposites! The dump() function needs two things: what data to save, and which file to save it to.
coding_requirements: Inside your save_inventory method's 'with' block, use json.dump() to write self.inventory to the file
Pass self.inventory as the first argument and the file object as the second argument
Make sure you already have 'import json' at the top of your file from earlier milestones
hints: The syntax is: json.dump(data_to_save, file_object)
Your file object is whatever variable name you used after 'as' in your with statement
Don't confuse json.dump() with json.dumps() - dump() writes to files, dumps() creates a string

We can add an 'indent' parameter to make it pretty-print with nice spacing. Setting indent=2 means each nested level gets 2 spaces of indentation. This doesn't change how the data works - it just makes it easier for humans (like you!) to read the file later.
